name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (iwasm); Wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (xmrsplayer audio, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max (A12) E-cores.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), M4 Max E-cores: wasm3 1.01, WAMR fast-interp 1.63, Wasmtime Pulley 2.09, WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; A12 E-cores: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68, WasmEdge 9.28. About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4 (derived from page data). Page text: 'wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0), no WASI sources; WAMR cmake Release -O3 FAST_INTERP only (AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off); Pulley rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with no JIT or AOT tier: far slower than compiling runtimes. In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is wasm3 16.51x vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x. Very cheap startup: same suite startup geomean wasm3 lazy 2.77x vs WAMR fast-interp 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the benchmark tested it supports only tail calls and extended-const. Maintainer states the project is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Benchmark author built WAMR with 29 carried patches and Pulley from a fork branch with 9 extra commits; all configurations are interpreter-only, so this is not a win over JIT/AOT Wasmtime, Wasmer or V8 (and wasm3 loses to them in the wasmi suite). Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. wasm3 instantiation of extended-const modules costs 62-122x Pulley's time. wasm3's own docs/Performance.md CoreMark table (wasm3 1627.87 vs wasm-micro-runtime 201.61, 8.1x) is dated 2019-2020 and labelled historical by the project. Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): WAMR fast-interp slower than wasm3 on every test, native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR; I derived about 1.5x wasm3 over WAMR from the per-test logs.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ WebAssembly runtime interpreter faster than wasmtime wasmer WAMR benchmark' led to wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks; WebSearch 'new WebAssembly interpreter 2026 ... wasm3 WAMR toywasm' led to rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark whose runtime-comparison doc holds the numbers.

name: toywasm
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter, V8, Wasmer and Wasmtime (startup); WAMR classic interpreter (ffmpeg execution)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup benchmarks (compile plus instantiate of bz2, pulldown-cmark, spidermonkey, ffmpeg, coremark, argon2 and erc20 modules), geomean of per-test time relative to the fastest runtime on each test, AMD EPYC 7763.
claimed_speedup: Startup geomean relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), EPYC 7763: Toywasm 18.35x vs WAMR fast-interpreter 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x (about 3.1x lower than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data). Toywasm is below WAMR fast-interp and below V8 on all five CPU data sets in the plots repo (e.g. Apple M2 Pro 16.38x vs WAMR 49.35x and V8 16.97x).
compiler_and_flags: C runtime built through the toywasmx 0.2 crate inside wasmi-benchmarks (C flags not shown in the repo); Rust harness profile.bench lto=fat, codegen-units=1
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (also data sets for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7-7700, Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C)
tradeoffs: Slowest interpreter in the suite for execution: execute geomean 318.96x on EPYC 7763 vs WAMR fast-interp 17.07x and wasm3 16.51x. Design goal is in-place interpretation with low memory use and broad spec support, not speed; it does not do lazy validation by design.
caveats: Suite is maintained by the wasmi project (competing runtime) and plots are SVGs; values were read from the SVG text labels, with runtime names matched to values by position in the file. wasm3 (lazy) startup is 2.77x, far lower than toywasm. Author's own ffmpeg.wasm run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yamt/toywasm/HEAD/benchmark/ffmpeg.txt, MacBook Pro 2018, 2.2 GHz 6-core i7, compiler flags not stated): toywasm 65.02 s vs iwasm 2.4.4 classic interpreter 210.58 s (3.2x, derived), WasmEdge 0.17.0 interpreter 198.75 s, wazero interpreter 173.08 s, but slower than wasm3 18.43 s, iwasm fast interpreter 23.14 s and wasmi 29.56 s, and far slower than JIT runtimes (3.54-11.89 s). Same author's startup.csv: toywasm 0.18 s vs Wasmtime first run 4.87 s and Wasmer first run 4.56 s.
found_via: WebFetch github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks (surfaced by WebSearch 'C++ WebAssembly runtime interpreter faster than wasmtime wasmer WAMR benchmark') and github.com/yamt/toywasm benchmark docs.

name: Fizzy
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter, V8, Wasmer and Wasmtime (startup); WABT wasm-interp (execution, not in list)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup benchmarks (compile plus instantiate of bz2, pulldown-cmark, spidermonkey, ffmpeg, coremark, argon2, erc20), geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test, AMD EPYC 7763.
claimed_speedup: Startup geomean relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), EPYC 7763: Fizzy 17.83x vs WAMR fast-interpreter 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x (about 3.2x lower than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ runtime built through the fizzyx 0.1.1 crate inside wasmi-benchmarks (flags not shown in the repo); the Fizzy README's own performance builds use Release -O3 with LTO and libstdc++
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (also data sets for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7-7700, Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C)
tradeoffs: README goals: clean C++17 with no external dependencies, interpreter only, WebAssembly 1.0 only (none of the proposals), deterministic behaviour for blockchain use. Execution speed is mid-pack: execute geomean 45.63x on EPYC 7763 vs WAMR fast-interp 17.07x and wasm3 16.51x.
caveats: Latest commit is a README PR merge, so code activity is probably older. Fizzy's own CHANGELOG (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmx/fizzy/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md, v0.5.0 detailed results, hardware not stated) shows execution about 5.1x faster than WABT 1.0.19 (WABT 508% of Fizzy time, derived) but wasm3 0.4.7 at 26% of Fizzy's execution time and 27% of its instantiation time, i.e. wasm3 is faster. Fizzy failed in Frank Denis's libsodium 2021-Q1 run (needs WASI poll_oneoff). Plot values read from SVG labels matched positionally.
found_via: WebFetch github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks and the wasmi-benchmarks-plots data directory (surfaced by WebSearch 'C++ WebAssembly runtime interpreter faster than wasmtime wasmer WAMR benchmark'); CHANGELOG from github.com/wasmx/fizzy.

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR)
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter (A-tier numbers); Wasmtime, Wasmer and V8 JIT/AOT (libsodium suite)
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (audio, graphql, DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max E-cores; WAMR configured as fast interpreter only.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), M4 Max E-cores: WAMR fast-interp 1.63 vs Wasmtime Pulley 2.09 and WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; A12 E-cores: WAMR 1.38 vs Pulley 1.68 and WasmEdge 9.28. About 1.28x faster than Pulley on the M4 and 1.22x on the A12 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: WAMR main (WAMR-2.4.1-364, b70d708d) cmake Release -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 with INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0; Pulley rust nightly-2026-07-05 --cfg=pulley_tail_calls fat LTO; Apple clang 21.0.0
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Configurable runtime (classic and fast interpreter, AOT via wamrc, Fast JIT, LLVM JIT); README lists small text sizes on cortex-m4f (about 58.9K fast interpreter, 56.3K classic interpreter, 29.4K AOT runtime). The fast interpreter is slower than wasm3 (1.63x vs 1.01x in the cited doc).
caveats: WAMR is itself a category baseline; listed for its measured wins over Wasmtime's Pulley interpreter and, in AOT mode, over JIT runtimes. The benchmarked WAMR carries 29 patches by the benchmark author (legacy EH, relaxed SIMD, PROT_NONE linear memory) and the Pulley side is a fork with 9 extra commits. AOT evidence (derived from page data): in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12 libsodium CSVs (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2022-12/res/iwasm.csv with wasmtime.csv, wasmer-cranelift.csv, wasmer-llvm.csv, node.csv, native.csv) the iwasm geomean time over 61 tests is 0.665x Wasmtime, 0.688x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.794x Wasmer LLVM and 0.588x Node/V8, and 2.30x native; the CSVs do not say iwasm ran in AOT mode (inferred from magnitude; CPU and flags not in the repo). WAMR wiki (https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/wiki/Performance, i7-7700, GCC 7.5.0 -O3, 2020-09-01) compares only against wasm3 and native.
found_via: WebSearch 'new WebAssembly interpreter 2026 ... wasm3 WAMR toywasm' led to rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark; jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks via github.com/topics/webassembly-runtime.

name: WAVM
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer (LLVM, Cranelift, Singlepass backends) and V8 (Node.js)
workload: libsodium 1.0.18 built to WASI (clang 11.1.0, wasm-opt -O4) and run on every runtime with ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; per-test timings across the crypto and codec test suite.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark author: 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test'; about 15% faster than Wasmer's LLVM backend; V8 (Node) second.
compiler_and_flags: Runtimes built from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode; guest built with system LLVM 11.1.0 and pre-optimised with wasm-opt -O4; same Wasm files for all runtimes; native and Wasm built with the same default flags
hardware: macOS x86_64 laptop (CPU model not stated) and a Linux x86_64 machine for the LLVM-runtime comparison
tradeoffs: LLVM-based compilation: the EOS VM README (github.com/AntelopeIO/eos-vm) calls WAVM compilation times 'extremely long and unpredictable'; LLVM dependency.
caveats: 2021 data; Wasmtime and Wasmer have changed since. The README's figures are in PNG charts, so the headline text is the claim; I also derived from the per-test logs (2021-Q1/output/macos-x86_64/*/*.log, 43 common tests, first log line as the time, unit and scope not stated) a geomean WAVM time of 0.68x Wasmtime, 0.82x Node/V8 and 0.98x Wasmer LLVM (so the 15% claim over Wasmer LLVM does not reproduce from those logs, which may include compile time). Frank Denis's 2026-06 post (search snippet only; 00f.net is blocked) says WAVM has the best optimizer and produced the fastest 2026 baseline number.
found_via: WebSearch 'github WebAssembly runtime written in C++ OR C faster than Wasmer or Wasmtime AOT JIT' snippet quoting the 2021-Q1 benchmark; jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2021-Q1 README.

name: wasm2c (WABT)
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer (Cranelift, LLVM, Singlepass) and V8 (Node.js)
workload: libsodium benchmark suite, 2022-12 run: 61 tests with results for every listed runtime plus native; wasm2c translates Wasm to C which is then compiled natively.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (wasm2c.csv vs the other runtimes' CSVs, geomean of per-test time ratios over 61 tests): wasm2c 0.68x Wasmtime, 0.71x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.82x Wasmer LLVM, 0.61x Node/V8, 0.22x Wasmer Singlepass; wasm2c geomean 2.36x native vs Wasmtime 3.46x, Wasmer Cranelift 3.34x, Node 3.91x.
stars_or_usage: 8.1k stars (WABT toolkit; wasm2c is one tool in it)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time only: the generated C must be compiled by a C compiler per module, so no JIT and an extra build step. Optional Segue optimisation (Linux x86-64, clang with -mfsgsbase) and optional extra sanity checks (WASM_RT_SANITY_CHECKS, high overhead, meant for debug builds) are described in wasm2c/README.md.
caveats: The results repo has no compiler, flags or CPU model for the 2022-12 run (methodology lives in the blocked 00f.net post), and the CSV unit is not stated, so only ratios are used. Frank Denis's 2026 post (search snippet only, 00f.net blocked) reports wasm2c built with zig cc -O3 -march=native at 0.814x Wasmtime and 0.887x Wasmer geomean with wide_arithmetic, and WAMR AOT at about 1.57x native. The wasm2c C-compile step is not part of the measured time.
found_via: WebSearch 'wasm2c w2c2 translate WebAssembly to C faster than wasmtime native speed benchmark'; jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12/res CSV files.

name: w2c2
workload: README CoreMark 1.0 of w2c2-translated C against native; the Wasmtime comparison is a libsodium benchmark reported in a blocked blog post.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Coremark 1.0: ~7% slower than native'. Blog (search snippet only, not on benchmark_url): libsodium benchmark Wasmtime 124.76 s vs w2c2-translated and compiled 73.38 s; CoreMark w2c2 2-5% slower than Wastrel which is 2-5% slower than native, Wasmtime 30-40% slower than GCC.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time Wasm to portable C translator (inspired by wabt wasm2c): output must be compiled per module; runs on many OSes and architectures including big-endian; WASI and threads support; no JIT.
caveats: No compiler, flags or CPU stated anywhere I could open; the Wasmtime numbers are from a search-result snippet of Frank Denis's 2023-12 post (00f.net blocked) so unverified. README gives no baseline runtime for the CoreMark figure.
found_via: WebSearch 'wasm2c w2c2 translate WebAssembly to C faster than wasmtime native speed benchmark'; github.com/turbolent/w2c2 README.

name: WasmEdge
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer (Cranelift, LLVM, Singlepass), V8 (Node.js) and wazero
workload: libsodium benchmark suite, 2022-12 run: 61 tests with results for every listed runtime plus native.
claimed_speedup: README: 'the fastest Wasm VM'. Derived from page data (wasmedge.csv vs the other CSVs, geomean per-test time ratio over 61 tests): WasmEdge 0.97x Wasmtime, 1.00x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.86x Node/V8, 0.31x Wasmer Singlepass, 0.21x wazero; 1.16x slower than Wasmer LLVM; geomean 3.35x native.
tradeoffs: Speed needs the LLVM-based AOT compiler step; the interpreter mode is among the slowest: geomean 8.42x the fastest on the M4 Max E-cores (REB doc) and 145.74x vs 1.15x for Wasmtime Cranelift on EPYC 7763 in the wasmi-benchmarks execute plot. Large dependency footprint.
caveats: Only parity with Wasmtime (3% within noise) and slower than Wasmer LLVM in the cited data; the README claim rests on a 2021 IEEE Software paper about serverless design that I did not open. The CSVs do not say whether WasmEdge ran in AOT mode (inferred from the 3.35x-native magnitude); CPU and flags unknown. Interpreter-mode numbers: https://github.com/rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark/blob/main/docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md.

name: libriscv
workload: README: cost to call a guest function and return (rainbow colour calculation with 3x sinf as the example) in an embedded sandbox, plus CoreMark and STREAM runs of the RISC-V emulator against native and wasm3.
claimed_speedup: README: 3 ns to call a VM function and return vs about 50-150 ns for other emulators; 'libriscv can call the above function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once'; CoreMark 38223 vs 41382 native (about 92%) with binary translation; interpreter mode 'substantially faster than other interpreters' (charts only).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7950X and Ryzen 6860Z (named in chart captions)
tradeoffs: Guests must be compiled to RISC-V (cross-compiler needed), not WebAssembly, so Wasm tooling does not apply; the README describes binary translation through DLLs or embedded translated code and an optional libtcc mode; designed for game-script sandboxing and low call latency.
caveats: Comparison charts are images and the wasmtime figure has no stated hardware, flags or Wasmtime version; benchmark author notes most benchmarks are hand-picked for game scripting. Author's gist (https://gist.github.com/fwsGonzo/9132f0ef7d3f009baa5b222eedf392da, hardware not stated) shows libriscv with TCC median 2 ns call vs LuaJIT 156 ns, but LuaJIT faster on taylor(1K) (858 ns vs 2234 ns). The README's wasmtime comparison is latency only.
found_via: WebFetch github.com/libriscv/libriscv after considering bytecode VM sandboxes besides Wasm.

name: WasmNow
baseline: V8 Liftoff baseline compiler and Wasmer Singlepass
workload: Copy-and-patch baseline compiler for WebAssembly measured on CoreMark and PolyBenchC: compilation speed and speed of the generated code.
claimed_speedup: README: compared with Chrome's Liftoff on CoreMark, compiles 5x faster while generating 39% faster code; on PolyBenchC, 6.5x faster compilation and 63% faster generated code.
tradeoffs: Research prototype: Wasm 1.0 core only, partial WASI, Linux only, builds through a Docker-based pochivm build system; README warns not to run untrusted Wasm because the JIT was never audited or fuzzed.
caveats: Numbers are from the project README; the OOPSLA 2021 Copy-and-Patch paper (Distinguished Paper) that the README cites was not opened (fredrikbk.com is blocked here), so a verifier with paper access may upgrade this to B. README states no hardware or compiler flags. Wasmer Singlepass is named as a baseline but no figures for it are on the page.
found_via: WebSearch 'github wasm JIT compiler C++ fast startup single-pass baseline compiler benchmark compared to wasmtime winch liftoff'.

name: WARP WebAssembly compiler (wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler)
baseline: V8 Liftoff and TurboFan (also SpiderMonkey Baseline and Ion)
workload: Single-pass Wasm compiler and runtime for embedded systems; README quadrant chart of normalised compilation speed and execution speed against browser engines, benchmark inputs from Schleifner/open-wasm-compiler-benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README quadrant chart (normalised, higher is better), compilation speed / execution speed: WARP 0.8316 / 0.8172; V8 Liftoff 0.747 / 0.4275; V8 TurboFan 0.0423 / 0.8505; SpiderMonkey Baseline 0.8136 / 0.3456; SpiderMonkey Ion 0.099 / 0.8163. README: 'Industry leading compilation speed and close to native execution speed'.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark guide builds vb_bench with clang/clang++ cmake Release, -DINTERRUPTION_REQUEST=0 -DEAGER_ALLOCATION=1; V8 x64.release and SpiderMonkey optimized builds (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler/develop/scripts/benchmark/Readme.md)
tradeoffs: Targets embedded and safety-critical use (AUTOSAR C++14, MISRA C++, no recursion, TriCore support); Wasm MVP plus some 2.0 features, no imported globals, tables or memories, no non-trapping float-to-int conversions.
caveats: Chart values are normalised scores with no raw timings, CPU model or workload list on the README page; the compared engines are browser JITs, not Wasmtime or Wasmer. WARP essentially ties TurboFan and Ion on execution (0.8172 vs 0.8505 and 0.8163) while compiling far faster, and ties SpiderMonkey Baseline on compile speed.
found_via: WebSearch 'github wasm JIT compiler C++ fast startup single-pass baseline compiler benchmark compared to wasmtime winch liftoff'.
